..The weekend is here and we are already starting to 
feel the changes coming our way. Tropical Storm Rachel has been 
pushing to the northeast at a good pace and is starting to interact 
with a trough/cut-off low over the Pacific. Additionally, a 
deepening trough is pushing down from the Pacific Northwest and will 
become a factor in the weather through the next several days. These 
features will all move towards southern California, with 
Rachel/trough moving into the SoCal coast through today, likely 
making landfall late tonight. The PacNW trough will then continue to 
dig further south, eventually moving over the Great Basin by early 
next week. The trough is slow to eject and may remain near the 
region through at least the middle of the week, potentially longer. 
Overall, an active weather pattern remains in play for the coming 
days. 

Today through Wednesday...Models have trended slightly west with 
the landfall of Rachel and the track of the remnants. This doesn't 
mean that we will be spared from the impacts, just that some of the 
higher impacts will shift westward. Moisture is already starting to 
stream into the region on the strengthening south to southwest flow. 
Some isolated showers and thunderstorms have developed and will 
continue to move towards the northeast through the night and into 
the morning hours. As we head through today, moisture will continue 
to increase and showers and thunderstorms will become more scattered 
to widespread. As moisture steadily increases, coverage of storm 
activity will also increase with Sunday and Monday looking to be the 
most active days, especially across western and southern areas where 
we currently have a Flood Watch in place.

QPF continue to be largely in the 1-3" range, with locally higher 
amounts are possible. With the path of Rachel shifting west, the 
best chances for the higher amounts mainly along and south of 
terrain features, mainly from the Grand Canyon down through the 
Mogollon Rim. There is still considerable uncertainty with how this 
event will unfold. Latest model runs show a bit more dry air being 
dragged into the mid-levels, which could potentially limit the heavy 
rainfall potential and keep storm activity more scattered and 
flooding more localized. But with cold air aloft, we may end up 
seeing some enhancement of rainfall rates, especially across higher 
terrain. Hi-res models continue to show multiple convective bands 
moving through the region over the next few days, with the potential 
for some to have some very heavy rainfall. Storms may be moving 
pretty quickly which could help to limit some potential flash 
flooding but will bear watching. Another thing to keep in mind is 
there will be decent instability available as the trough pushes into 
the Desert Southwest. Combined with the ample moisture and deep 
shear there will be the potential for some supercells to develop 
with strong/damaging winds being the main hazard. 

Winds will also be an issue with these systems. Expect increasing 
south to southwest winds as the gradient tightens up in advance of 
Rachel's landfall, then further tightening as the remnants/trough 
move across the area. Winds look to be strongest on Sunday and Wind 
Advisory is in effect for the entire area. Winds may remain elevated 
on Monday and the advisory may need to be extended for portions of 
the forecast area.  Winds on Sunday will be south to southwest 25-35 
mph with gusts 40-50 mph with some locally higher gusts possible. 
Winds remain strong on Monday and Tuesday, mainly across the higher 
terrain but really begin to taper off later Tuesday. 

There is some conflict in the models on just what transpires with 
the PacNW trough in the midweek time frame. Will it eject out around 
Wednesday or become a cut off low that stalls nearby through the end 
of the week? Only time will tell and hopefully the models will come 
to an agreement in the coming days.
